blocks.x: What about your life first, Punch? Yeah.
Time now?

Yeah, go ahead. Well, I was born at Race in Louisiana sometime back in that floor out of New Orleans. And just as soon as I got out of school, well, I left that place to come on into New Orleans. Where were you born? Race in Louisiana.
What year was that in you, on what day?
What was the date? When was your birthday?

Oh, let me see. June 14, 1894. After I got in New Orleans, I left from New Orleans, and the Army took me. From the Army back to New Orleans, and I still got married, and lived with my wife six years, and I left here in 27 for Chicago. And I stayed in Chicago up until 51. And from that, well, I just been running around different bands, played in nice places, nice spots. I did pretty good all of my life. So, thought I'd come on back to the old stomping ground, spend a while here again. I think that's a good idea, don't you?
Yeah.

Very good idea. So, my first man I worked with here was a fellow named Jack Kerri. We supposed to invent a tagger rag. And we did very nice around New Orleans, so some of the boys in the band decided me to get my own band, such as George Boyd, Walter Preston, Joe Gable, and Aidy Morris. And we got a little band together there, and we really did fine, fine, until the same thing like now, come up Lent, and we all got a job. I didn't have any when I called them to play. They couldn't go. So, I just thought I'd move on up. And I left and hit the road. And I've been on the road all this time up until now. And I've played with many things. Converse, circus, stage shows, all kind of things. Rodeos and everything a man can name, I played it, you know. And all kind of spots in Chicago.
Now tell us, how did you get your name Punch? How did you get that nickname?
Oh, that nickname was from twins. We were twins. My sister's name, Ernestine Judy Miller, and my name is Ernest Punch Miller. So that's why we got the name. They called us Punch and Judy.
Is that a real middle name Judy?
Yeah, that's a real middle name. That's no joke. She's still living? No, my sister died in 1926. I left right after she died.
Can you tell us about your father? Did he play any instrument?

Well, no. My father didn't, which I didn't ever know him, because he left when we were kids. But my mother was a mighty good singer in church. And she told a lot of people she thought I'd turn out to be a fine singer. She didn't know what, but she told them that I'd turn out to be somebody good.
You'd know how to be a fine musician.
And she gave me to my uncle, and my uncle brought me up, and after he brought me up, well, I did.
Did he play anything?

No, none of them. I'll tell you how I got my style. The old men out of our home had a brass band. Well, I decided to buy all new instruments. And every man that had a son or any kind of relation was a kid, they give him the instrument, the old instrument. So, well, best I could do was pick up on a bass drum. But I was so apt picking up different instruments and playing them. Some of the boys told me they'd better put me on baritone. I played that pretty good. Next thing I learned, I was on the trumpet, which cornet in them days. How old were you about it? Oh, we always in our teens. We was young, very young teens.
And still over at Raceland?

Raceland, Louisiana, yeah. And so, a fellow by the name of Paul Rozier, like eight miles from my home, he picked up on me and brought me in his band. He had a band there, and I used to play with him all the time. Another fellow named Mike Taylor, one mile from there. And Nick's a fellow from here. Not from here. He's from Raceland, but he's an older man to me named Bo Bo. Used to be a tuba player way back there with Buddy Bowling. And he picked me up in Brompton, New Orleans, one time. And I come in and played a while, but I went back home again. I was very young then. And stuff like stuff stuff like stuff So, you know, I've heard it did now, but I know I'm explaining everything just how it was. So, when I first got away from that fellow by the name of Billy Mack, they had a shooter called the Miramack Makers. And when he got to New Orleans, he didn't have no trumpet player, so he asked me to play the show with him. So I played the show down with him, and from then on he asked me to go to Chicago.
Who else was in the band when you went up? Who else played in that band with you?
Well, they had a fellow named Wilbur Parrish, trombone, and a fellow named Brown, Henry Brown on piano. And, I'm trying to get back on it now, I can't.
Where'd they come from? They weren't from New Orleans then?

Well, Parrish, fellow, he's from, I think of Georgia. And they had a fellow from Mississippi, he's named Jackson. He played in the band. Old, there was fellows that I kind of slipped my remembrance now, but I, you know. Jackson, what did you do? Well, none of them was from New Orleans, not them.
That piano player, Henry Brown? Henry Brown.
Do you know where he came from?
No. What type of music did you play in the show, all sorts of?

Well, music for the chorus, the dance bar, and tap dance music, and music for the singer. Then the comedian named Henry Reno, he, you know, we should play some songs and things for him. And Billy Mack, well, he had all his own songs. Hard Luck was one of his songs. Yeah. Black But Sweet Old God. That's when you made a record. And Miss Mack, and had another lady with her by the name of Mary Evans, and they did a number by the call of Bear. It was a beautiful thing, too, Bear. That was the name of her, Bear, but the way they sang it, huh?
Bear what?
Bear, Bear, Biddlem. Yeah, that's what's the name of the song, Bear, Bear, Bear, Biddlem. Oh, it was really good, so. I did all right.
Did you say music in the show, did you have to read music, or did they just read everything?

Well, they did have a little music scratched out, but I wasn't such a good reader then. This fellow trombone player, he was a mighty good musician, Wilbert Parrish. He had a brother named Sidney Parrish, you might have heard of him.
Well, he was real musicians.

In New York, no. There was a funny thing about that. I used to make some kind of run all the time on my horn, and Wilbert sat down and rode it out for me. And they asked me to play again. I said, I can't play again, man. He said, well, that's what you make on your horn all the time. It was funny, but, you know, then times. And I stayed in Houston, Texas a long time with a fellow by the name of Frank Davis. I stood there a long time. Did he have a show, or was he a band leader? No, he had a band, a dance band. What did he play? He was a drummer. Drummer.
Was there a fellow named Franky Gibbs? Gibbs, he's playing trombone with us.
Crippled trombone player. Yeah, Bunkett, you talked about him.
One leg was shorter than the other.
Yeah, one leg was shorter than the other. Was he any good? Oh yeah, he's a nice musician.
Good trombone player. He may still be there. One night we went out.
We weren't playing. Another band was playing.
So he was sitting down, and a lady came up, and she asked him to dance. So he kept telling me he didn't want to dance, but she kept insisting.
One leg shodd another.
One leg shodd another. One leg shodd another.

One leg shodd another. One leg shodd another. One leg shodd another. Yeah, one leg shodd another. Yeah, one leg shodd another. Was he any good? Was he any good? Oh yeah, he's a nice musician. Good trombone player. One night we went out. We weren't playing, another band was playing, so he was sitting down, and a lady came up, and she asked him to dance. So he kept telling me he didn't want to dance, but she kept insisting. So when he got up to dance, she asked him, what was he doing, shouting? One leg shodd another. And he said, no. He said, I told you I didn't know how to dance. I just got one leg shodd another. She said, oh excuse me, I thought you were shouting or doing something like that. So that was just a little joke, you know, but it was true. Yeah. And I don't know, so many other good things I did. When did you get here?
What about, which year was it, right before the war you stayed?

I came here a couple of times before the war, but I didn't stay here. I went back, back in the country. But in my main time, when I came here to stay, after I left the Army. And I came on here and stood until 1926. Went on into Chicago.
You remember some of the other good musicians around here? You said you played in Jack Carey's band. Who were some of the other bands, the other trumpet players you heard when you first came here?

When I first came here? Yeah. Well, Buddy Petit was one of the fellas, Ray and Plinistain. And Kid René. And Louis too, Louis Armstrong. He was cracking them up. But the idea about Louis, he always played off like the Capitol Boat. And going off something, you know, like that. He'd play in brass bands every now and then, but he wasn't exactly with us, because he always looked like a little above that, or some kind of really. Yeah. Big time people would hire him all the time, you know. He'd work with a kid, Ori, around here. That's when I first met him. I went down to 25. I just got out of the Army, and Louis was playing with Ori. So, Ori and Johnny Dotson, him. So, they invited me up to play a piece, and I played a piece, and they got the kid in Louis about it. So Louis told him, so let him take my place. I cut out. I said, no, we're just kidding. You know, this was a joke.
Louis thought you meant it though, huh, did he? Yeah. Louis thought they were going to hire you in this place?

Yeah, he thought it for a while, but he was just kidding. I brought a piece back from the Army, and who had it called, Over There? Yeah. And I really could play that piece. They hadn't heard it. Yeah, it was good. Yeah, I remember.
Yeah. Did you hear Keppert when you...
Keppert?
Freddie Keppert? Yeah.
I worked with him in Chicago.
Oh, you were up in Chicago?
Yeah, at the Dreamland.
You never played with him down here?
No, I never played with him down here. First time I met him was in Chicago.
Did you ever hear bunk when you were a boy here?

Well, yes. I'll tell you how I heard bunk. I was in the country, and the excursion was going from New Orleans to Homer, Louisiana, and I caught the excursion at a race, and they went to Homer and stood right by him all day, listening to them blokes. That's how I met him.
Now, you never got to hear Bolden, I guess. No, Bolden, no.
He was the head of my time.
Yeah.
Did you ever work with Big I.
Louis? Big I. Louis? Well, I never worked with him, but I knowed him.
I knowed him.
I worked with Manuel Mineta, though.
Oh, yeah?
Oh, yes, indeed. We worked together a good while.
In whose band?
Well, to tell the truth, he played with me in my band. I had a band. He worked with me. Then a couple of times he worked with Jack Carey. Who?
What was he playing in those days?
He was playing, let's see what he was playing there. Piano. Piano, yeah, piano.
Who was in Jack Carey's band, ordinarily?
Well, they had a little fella on drumming called Chinee.
Yeah, I know him.

Jack Carey on trombone, I was on trumpet. And they had, first they had a boy on a kind of name Robeshow. He was kind of this old man Robeshow, but he was a young fella. Then after that, George Boyd come in there with him. And I don't know who Jack, I mean Jack had on bass. Oh, yeah, Chester. Chester Zadis. That's who he had on bass violin. So, when I got in my band, for some reason I had George Boyd, Aiden Morris, Joe Gable on bass, Walter Preston on guitar, and me on trumpet.
Who was guitar with Carey? What did you say? With Carey?
Yeah. Tom Benton most of the time.
Oh, yeah, I met him once. Yeah, Tom Benton.
Where's the other one? Well, a couple of times Lorenzo Stahl played with us too.
Did he sing? Stahl?
Lorenzo?
No, he didn't sing.
He used to sing.
He used to sing.
He used to be funny though, I'll tell you that. Yeah.
Yeah, I heard somebody tell some old tune he used to sing sometimes after he'd been drinking or something like that.
Yeah, well, he'd do them kind of things.
More funny than singing, I guess.

He tickled me one time. Some people hired Jack Carey to go to Birmingham and play for a night. Yeah, one night and a day. That's how it was, one night and a day. And he'd give each man a hundred dollars a piece in transportation. So, Road Runners are so funny. When Jack Carey got ready to pay us off, he asked Jack, say, you gonna give that clan that play a hundred dollars? So, Jack said, yeah, why? He said, man, give me half of his money because I'm sitting up there playing all that nice banjo and he's sitting up there with that clan that talking about I will follow where he lead it. That was a funny thing, but it was real funny when he did that. And Road Show was a young kid, you know. He looked like he wanted to cry.
How many years were you with Carey?
Hmm?
With Jack Carey.
I worked with Carey, Carey just about three years. Yeah, about three years.
And how many years did you have your own band out here?
About four years. Well, you could easily count it. I come back in 1919 and I worked with Jack Carey. Then I left here in 26. From 1919 to 26.
Yeah, that would add up to him. Hmm? That adds up about right. It worked out time.
Well, someplace I read you were, you played with Fate Narrable too. Did you play on the play?

Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. I played Vindoon with Fate a couple of Sundays after Lewis left, Chicago went to New York. Yeah. Well, they hired me and I taken Lewis place. And worked with him. Another funny thing about that.
Who was Fate Narrable?

Oh, Fate Narrable. I think, tell me, Erskine Tate. Erskine Tate, no. No, that's in Chicago. Yeah, yeah. No, Fate Narrable. I just played with him on one trip. One trip, I knew. You just go up the river with him. Yeah, yeah. One trip.
How long did that go? A month or so? Mm-hmm. How long? Not all summer?
No, no, no. We left on, I think, on a Saturday night and come back on a Tuesday. Oh yeah.
Yeah.

Sorry. I was going to tell you about this fellow in Chicago, I just called his name, Erskine Tate. Yeah, I mentioned that. Let me tell you. I was taking Lewis place with him and, see I had never been to the Vindu, and when you take a solo, that spotlight right over your head like that, see. And so there was playing the center of his blues, and he told me, he said, now Punch, and I went, as soon as the saxophone player finishes course, you jump right up and light out. I said, okay. And I didn't know that light was up there, see. So as soon as I jumped up, the light come on. And boy, there was it. I got to about a minute before I could get straight. That light was really scary. Sure, it was so low, right to your head. See, it hit, boop, like that, all that work. And I'm telling you.
Yeah, it was.

But we had a lovely band at the Golden Lill in Chicago. We had five years, like one spot. A boy named little Francois Mosley had the band, and the place caught a fire on a Saturday night. That's how we got out of job there. But we would have been there, I guess, for 10 years. That was a nice job.
Who was in the band ready to go to the world?

Well, a fellow on guitar named Charles Ducasten. A big stout fellow played clarinet and saxophone named Fred Howard. And Fred Reeves on the piano. I was on the trumpet. Francois was on the drums. And we had Al Wins a lot of different times. Now, I'll tell you who worked with us there a long time. People would not believe that, but it's true. You heard of Ted Wilson? Oh, yeah. Well, he worked right there with us a long time after he left his dorm. Oh, no. Did you know that band from Kansas City? A fellow that died had that band from Kansas City. I don't know. Moatland and? Hmm? Moatland. Yeah, what he named? Moatland. Lee Moatland. Yeah, yeah. He worked with Van Moatland.
I don't know anything about that. Ted did.
Yeah, Ted. And when he come in Chicago, he come join us. He's been with us a long time. Ted Wilson. Yeah.
Somebody once told me you worked with the Jelly Roll on the road.

Oh, yeah, I worked with Jelly. About, well, I went out two years with him. That's how I worked. See, Jelly, he would, in the wintertime, he'd take a band out. He'd go all over. Well, summer, he'd keep band together, but he wouldn't do much playing in the summer. But, I went out two years with him like that, the same way I did with Walter Barnes. He'd go out for the winter all down Florida and everywhere. But, when he'd come back, he had a big grocery in Chicago. Barnes, huh?
Barnes, Walter Barnes? Yeah, Walter Barnes.

And all the summer, he'd stay in the grocery. In the wintertime, come, he'd make up a band again and go out. Well, that's how come I wanted to fire, because when he made that last trip, I had a job in Chicago, and I didn't come out with him. And that's when that happened.
Can you tell us something more about Jelly? Who was in the band when you...

Well, there's one fellow I can remember, because me and him used to bum together. I would call him King Porter. He was a trumpet player, too. He played first trumpet. Me and him used to bum together. Now, the other fellows, really, I don't forgot the names and things, you know. I really have.
About what year was that?
Oh, this was about in, I'd say about in 31, 32, something like that.
Pretty late then, if he'd been in Chicago a couple of years.
Yeah. Did you ever know a trumpet player? I think he was from, well, he played around Texas. His name was King Swayze.
Well, that's what I'm talking about. King Swayze.
Yeah.

But I said King Porter, didn't he? Yeah. No, King Swayze, tall, slender boy. Yeah, not too honest. That's what I am to say. Yeah, I wasn't. King Swayze, yeah. King Porter, I know him too. He's in Detroit. And what does he play?
Trumpet.
Big stout fella from Birmingham, Alabama. I played with him on shows.
How old would he be King Porter? King Porter? The trumpet player, yeah.
King Porter. Well, he's younger than I am. He must be somewhere like about 50, he's close around 58 now. He's younger than I am.
Tell us about Heinz. Did you ever play with Earl Heinz?
Well, I'll tell you how it happened. Just one time I played with him. I was taking a boy at a place there named Jabo.
Oh, Jabo Smith?
Yeah, Jabo Smith. I worked with him one night and Jabo come back the next night. That was his job. He just got off somewhere and didn't show up.
Have you played, you say, with Earl Wynn, you hadn't played with Earl Wynn down here, though? When did you?
In New Orleans? Yeah. No, first time I played with him was in Chicago. Yeah.

I have a Christmas card from Earl Wynn. I've been wanting to hunt it up and show you. I'll show it to you tomorrow night if I can find it down. I'll fix your hunt here. I've been intending to do that. You going to have you wrote him or you going to write him? No, I'm going to write him. I'll tell him to tell him about me. I will. I sure will.
And tell us more about Tiny Paar.
When did you meet him?
Well, Tiny Paar was at the Dreamland.

And this Cliff Jones, we call him Snag, he come up one day to my house and told me that Tiny Paar sent him to get me to play with him. So I went on down and made rehearsal with him and went through okay. So I went there at the Dreamland with him and then tell the truth, we come on down there and played dances. You know all in stuff.

Well, Tiny Palm was at the Dreamland and this Cliff Jones, we call him Snag, he come up one day to my house and told me that Tiny Palm sent him to get me to play with him. So I went on down and made rehearsal with him and went through okay. So I worked there at the Dreamland with him and then tell the truth, we come on down there and played dances, you know all these. Yeah, middle trip, all the way, you know, tour.
That's the State Street, the Dreamland on State Street.
Yeah, with the glass floor.
Yeah, I remember. Right there. They had a Westside, Greenland, too, you know, out there, Jimmy Nune and Shepard's and...
Oh yeah, I remember that. I remember that.
Charlie Cook, Greenland. Yeah. Now, who all was in the band? Can you remember a few of the people?

Well, I remember a couple of them, Snag and myself and Tiny and a fellow on trombone named Eddie Ellis. Eddie Ellis and they had the spore on alto. I believe you used to tell me about him, about his name today on the saxophone. Yeah, or Boone. Oh, Lester Boone.
Lester Boone.
Yeah.
He was on two different records with him when Al was in.
Yeah, well, he played with us, too, at the Dreamland with Tiny Pong. And there's Jimmy Suppen, Jimmy Suppen on bass violin.
Did he play tuba or just the string bass?
Oh, he played tuba and string bass.
Yeah.

Now, about the first real job I went on in Chicago, many people don't know it, but we were supposed to be the first band that went on the air. A fellow by the name of Hugh Swift. Oh, yeah. He had 16 pieces out of the place. They called Jeffrey Tavern. Chicago and Jeffrey.
Were you in the band when Baby played with him for Baby Dogs for a while?

Yeah, yeah, I took a little short boy's place there, and he lost his lip. His lip went bad on him. He couldn't play, and I took him this place. And they featured me maddy good. They featured me a lot there, singing and blowing. I worked there about a year with them, making nice money. I tell you, you ever heard of Junior Cobbs? Oh, yes. He was in the band. He played a lot of different instruments. Yeah, that's him. That's him. Well, he the one come and got me to go with that band. Because I was playing in a little place called The Bookstore, down on 31st Street. The same fellow Ted Wilson, old little, was playing piano there. And I was working there with her, and Junior Cobbs come and heard me play one night, and he goes back and tells Hugh Swift about me. So Hugh would have told him to bring me out to rehearsal. I would have to rehearse it with him. And I went right on to work with him. Oh, it was some nice days in Chicago for me.
Well, to get back to those Tiny Parham records, Dick, did you go over that list of which ones? Punch Resort, I remember some of those names. Different ones.

He's in the ensemble on Headhunter's Dream, but the solo, we figured, is Ray Hoffman. Just from this one. What about that last solo? Was there an ending on that? There's an ensemble on that, yes. And that's fun. Yeah, towards the end, yeah. And, uh, and solo trumpet on Stuttering Blues is him, and he's an ensemble trumpet too. He's on Jogo Rhythm, Cuckoo Blues he's on that. Mm-hmm. And Punch is playing second trumpet on Stomping On Down, and they go out, the last chorus. Yeah. And Skaggalag, the other trumpet player, takes the first solo, and the last solo is by Punch. Mm-hmm. Let's see. What else we got about? Are there any other old records you went over besides the Parham? Yeah, well there's more Parham. Oh, okay. Blue Island Blues, that's the other fella, Hopson. Let me see. John Locro, that's probably him, Hopson.

How big a band was that? Excuse me. Uh, Cathedral Blues. Tell the truth, I think I'm playing second trumpet there on all them records, but some of them I took solos on, see? Yeah. But I'm still playing second trumpet with all the records he made.

You hear the other trumpet playing on Dixieland Doings, and then right on the other side of that Cathedral Blues, you take a solo, so you can, a lot of times you can hear those two trumpets. And we played that Frisky Foot Jackson. What did you tell me about him? What did he play?
Drums.
He played drums. Yeah.
He really was the drummer, Frisky Foot Jackson, huh?
Yeah, that just wasn't a made up name. It was a real thing.
I thought that record came out on their, under another name, too. Yeah.

Like one of the Jimmy Blythe groups. Yeah, I think maybe it did. Uh, Cathedral Blues he's on, and Dixieland Doings the other side, it's another trouble. We thought maybe it was Frankie Halfbine with the vocal, but he can't hear too well.

Uh, do you know anything about Tiny Parham? I never did get to talk to him. I saw him play once at the Savoy Ballroom in 1938. Yeah. He's a big, big, fat doll was playing the organ. That's right. And I went over there with Mead Lux Lewis, and I said, who's the organist? He said, oh, everybody knows him. If you know him, that's Tiny. Yeah, that's right. A big, big, big fella.
Yeah.
But I didn't get to talk to him that night. Uh, did he come from Chicago, do you think, or where was he from?
Well, when I first saw him, he was living in Chicago, but really, with his home, I don't know if he was born in Chicago or not.
You never did hear him talk about one of them? No, never did. Because he died before anybody ever got to talk to him and find out about his life, I think.
Where did you first meet, uh, this fella, Lewis James, anyhow? Lewis James?
The bass player. Oh, I first met him right here. But no, no, I wouldn't say that. I believe I saw him some years back with Gabriel Vann out in the country.
Who was Gabriel?
Uh, Joe Gabriel. Oh, he used to have a sweet band out there. White folks was crazy about his music. That's out on Bally Fush, though.
Uh-huh. And you remember any of the other guys from Gabriel's band?
Nobody but Sean, the singer-boy, used to sing. And Joe, them one of the two I remember.
Were they, did they play writing music, or what?
No, they played sweet music.
They read, or? Hmm? Did they read, or did they play?
Oh, yeah, they read music, they were the real musicians.
Hmm.

Where, where were some of the places you played when you were down here? When you first, some of the old halls, or what kind of jobs? Oh, well. When you had your own band, or Jack Carey, where'd you play?

Well, when I was, Jack Carey played in National Park the most of the time. National Park? Yeah, yeah, that's 3rd and Willow. 3rd and Willow. They've got a big school up there now, big school there. And we'd go out in like Gulfport, Biloxi, and all up there in Magnolia, Mississippi towns like that and play. And after I got my band, we the first band opened up their stores, my band. First band went up there. The hotel, okay. Yes, up over that hotel there. And we worked there a long time for beans.

And then I played Cooperators, Economy, and Napoleon Avenue Hall up there. I forget the name of that hall. And played the Frazarmi. I played the Santa Sinners. Oh, I played Freshman Hall. I played all around down there.
Was there anything going on out of Mellenburg in your days?

Oh, every Sunday in your birth. Every Sunday I'd go out in your birth. I used to play for a lot of white boys, you know, at clubs and things. I played for them all the time. There was a fellow named Joe Gundolfi, an Italian boy. He kept me working all the time. Kept me busy all the time.
What were some of those halls? Did you ever work at St. Elizabeth?
Yeah, sure. That's the hall I tried to call. That's up above the Poirier Avenue. That's the one I tried to call, St. Elizabeth.
Well, it was the St. Catharines. Did you ever work over here by Tulane on the church? I don't know the church. Is that St. Catharines Church?
Yeah, there's a hall there called St. Catharines. Right across from the church. Yeah, but I never did play there.
I never worked there.
The fucking baby dog. Yeah, I never did play there.
What about the Million Willows? Did you ever hear that?
Well, that Million Willows. Million Willows.
The T. Thurden Willows. I think that's what it is. Yeah, Thurden Willows.
That's where the National Park was. The National Park.
Yeah, I mean we played there every Monday night, Sunday night. But what about Miss Cole's lawn parties?
I was just at Fing and Willows. Yeah, I played there a couple of times too. A little yard, you know? Yeah. I mean we played there every Monday night, Sunday night.
But what about Miss Cole's lawn parties?

That was just at Fing and Willows. Yeah, I played there a couple of times too. And used to have a little place right back of Perdita Street there. A little yard, you know? Yeah. Right there. Perdita and Satova, I think. It was a Franklin. One of them streets. But that's where Lewis used to get off the boat and come catch me playing there all the time to sit in and play with me.
Who ran that place? Was that?
Toodle-um. Toodle-um.
Yeah, Toodle-um. Yeah. Just on that page.
I was wondering, when you first started out, did you have any particular ideals that you patented yourself on?
Who did you like in particular? What trumpet player did you, inspired you?

Well, Buddy Petit was my idea all the time. I liked him all the time. All the time. Just like a lot of people say, I play and sing like Lewis. But I was doing that before Lewis started singing. I was singing the same way. The same way. I didn't pick up nothing after him. I just sing like that all the time. And Lewis told me one of these days he was going to tell the people that I always did sing like that. I'm not picking up nothing from him. See, he heard a lot of people say I patented after him, but I don't. Before Lewis started singing, I'd sing up on that store and all around and sing the same way.
What about your trumpet playing? Do you think you picked up anything off of Lewis or his record or anything? I just play my own weed.
Might sound like him, but I've been playing my own weed.
You always played this style more or less that you do now way back or did you ever change your style?
Well, no, it was a little different back.
Let me go ahead. You ask the first question. Can we talk about Jack Gary again? Yeah, that's what I'll do in that. Yeah. I was wondering what some of the tunes were that Jack Gary played.
Well, Taggerad, That's A Plenty, Honeysuckle Road, Kranath Marbley, and what else? I was wondering if you were a kid, you know, a lot of head numbers that we know ourselves. Number one, called one.

A lot of things I can't remember now, but— Do you remember number one? Oh, yeah, I remember that. I mean, could you hum a little bit of it for us so we could get the idea what the tune— You wouldn't mind?
No, but it's— Well, the kind of—it's bricks. See, the planet here, more than the way. It goes, . You know, yeah.
Does it have a name now? Did they put— Well, ain't nobody playing it now.

I wrote it for Sam. I don't know if he's gonna use it or not. Sam, you know, up there, I wrote it for him. I wish somebody could play it, but you gotta have a good clannery case, because it's got breaks all the way through. Even at the end of it, the clannery makes the end of it, and then we hit the last note.

It's a pretty nice piece. Did any of the tunes have any special names? Well, we call that number one. Yeah, but I mean like the Tiger Rag, did it have another name? Oh, Tiger Rag, that's all. We called it. Did it have any words? That's one thing.

Well, yeah, the people out in the audience started singing. When we were playing, when we got to that last spot, they said, Jack Carey on the water, selling pork chops, two for a quarter, you know. It just kept on going like that. They made a song, I assume. I couldn't remember it all. All I knew there was a party at the corner of Third Wood at a grocery store. And every time we'd go to the National Park on Monday nights past that, he started singing, Jack Carey, Harry Dog on the water. Jack Carey could sing that thing that's his playing his doing. A parrot, huh? A parrot, yeah. A parrot, yeah.
A parrot, yeah.

And it was really good in them days and times. I don't know. Bands meeting up and down the street, get on the corner like that, stay there two, three hours blowing at one another. Here'll come another band, three or four that day. That one play one, this one play one, you play. Oh boy, I was just talking them days. Well, you see those advertising in the halls, you know, different halls that they're going to play? It was like, you know, play at one hall, you're trying to draw the people, I'm trying to draw them, you're trying to draw them. This was one of them things. But it was all good in them days and times. Really good.
Who did you meet in the street, some of the different bands?

Well, every Sunday you'd meet a bunch, but it'd be the same bunch like Rene, Buddy Petit, Sam Marock, Chris Kelly, and what's his name? The Dine, downtown there, Cindy Desvinge, the old tuxedo, all them bands used to be out on the street, you know, advertising dances on Sundays. Maybe one of them would be playing at a funeral or something, somebody would die, and they'd all get on that together.
Did you ever have any battles of music in the places like, say, the Bows Club or any of those?

Well, I won two Cups, one at the Espinade Hall down there, against Chris Kelly. What's that, the Italian Hall? The Italian Hall, yeah, that's what it was, the Italian Hall, and I won another at the St. Elizabeth, off a band called, well it was Earl Humphrey had the band then, that George Washington was playing, and it used to have two bands and everybody had a little dance at them times. Two bands, one this corner. Earl Humphrey had a band with George Washington?
Earl Humphrey had a band with who in it?

He didn't have no band, just make up band for it, or for a gig they called it, you know. The gig was blowing to Earl, and Earl didn't have nobody play, so who, who just went around and picked up some fellas and went play the game, but just for eleven cups, see. And I lost one cup with Son of Silestan. And I played for three, and one, two, I had three, but he had such a big band, see, he had twelve pieces, and I had six pieces.

So that's where we all went. The Tiger Ragnar, did they ever call that play Jack Carey, or? Yeah, they used to say that too. Did they yell that as a break sometime, that play Jack Carey? I mean, the, over the, the.

No, they just were regular singing all over the dance floor, you could just young hollering, Jack Carey, head of daughter, on the water, selling pork chops, two folk quarters, play Jack Carey, play Jack Carey, all that guys, you know.
I wondered in that part that they, where the trombone gives the smear, and then they say, hold that tiger. Yeah, that's, that's the last part.

Did they say play Jack Carey for those words then? That part, that part where they say, hold, uh, play, uh, Jack Carey on the water, that's part go, da-da-da, da-da-da, da-da-da, da-da-da, that's the part where they sing. Jack Carey, head of daughter, seven pork chops, two folk quarter, you know, like that on, and we get to the last part that say, hold that tiger, hold that tiger, you know. That's one of them things. It was all good in them days and time.
Well, is anybody alive who plays much like Jack Carey, or any recordings that are much on his style?

Well, ain't but one guy that seems like Eddie Morris, probably the only one. Cause all the rest of them, probably, they, uh, the way they play trombone now, they feel like they play trompones. Yeah, they all play in the lead. Yeah, but Eddie Morris got more, you know, that style, playing sides and stuff, you know, sides. They had a fellow named Morris French. I don't know what would come of him. He's up in Laplace.
Laplace.
Laplace, huh? Well, he was one of Jack Carey's, you know, under-comped fellas. Jack Carey, he just liked Jack Carey, and he's played just like Jack Carey.

Well, there's somebody for us to dig that. Yeah. It's only about 20 or 30 miles up there. Huh? It's only about 20 or 30 miles up there. Yeah, yeah, that's pretty much crunchy. His nephew's playing with Solistan, and I played Daniel Albert. Yeah. He was Solistan now. Yeah, you know, Solistan's band is going. Oh, I know.
Well, where do they play?

Oh, they play a lot of stuff. Oh, I thought they were on Bourbon Street, you're not on the wharf. No, they play up on the wharf for the boats leaving and a lot of private answers and everything. The widow gets a child. That's true.
Can you remember the very first job you played that you got paid for? Was it in the country or in the city here?

Was in the country. Was in the country, right where I lived at. I was on a lawn. We got fifty cents a piece. And I got seventy-five cents. But the rest of them was, you know, fifty cents a piece. Plenty of money, too.
Were you in the leader or something?

Well, no, I just did all the work. We didn't have no leader. I was holding the band up. I said, they didn't give me the six bits. How old were you then, Doc? Well, I said I was sixteen. We was young. See, the old ones give us the band. They got new instruments. And everybody that had anybody relation to them, well, they just give them the instrument, they took the new instrument. So I didn't know quite in the band, so they just give me the bass drum. And I played it. Started to tune with them horns and I could play all of them. I just go on playing by head, but I could play them. So they gave me the trumpet. Baritone first, I played that, then I took the trumpet. And I come to find out a fellow from another town come grab me, and I went and play in this band. From then on, I just kept going. Old man named Paul Rose gave me my little start on music.

He did now, too. Some of these people weren't here last night when you were telling about your life. That was in Raceland? Raceland, yeah. When were you born? What was your birthday? 1894. The birthday is, uh... Exactly. December 9th. December. December 9th. December 9th. December 9th. Yeah. Right before Christmas. Yeah. Been a good while back. Yeah. Ninety- 1894. That's right.
Well, when you first started, were you reading music? No indeed. Entirely by- Hmm? Entirely by head.
By ear. That's when I'd whistle something up and pick the horn and blow it.
That's true about that.

I could just whistle something up and pick the horn up and blow it. I don't know what key I was on unless I knew I played. And, uh, who taught you how to read it? Well, I liked something in the Army. I stole my reading. That's the truth I stole. A fella named Chip used to be there. Yeah, he did. Now, you heard of him. His name was Lewis Mathis. He was one of his kid over at trumpet players way back years ago and called him Chip. Well, I was in the Army and I used to go on watching him. I had my music up there but I'm watching his fingers, see? Every time he'd touch a bass I'd touch one. So he said, uh-uh, you can't make it like that. He said, you better learn some music. So he started to show him. From then on, I just kept on. Old man Joe Howard was there. I come to him and I come to New Orleans and I stayed around him. And I got a little lesson from Willie Humphrey's daddy too. Which Willie Humphrey's daddy?
He's daddy, huh? Which, no, which Willie Humphrey? I mean there's a- The old man. Not Willie Humphrey would play the clarinet.
Well, both of them play clarinet. I know, but the old man, he's daddy. The old man Jim was a trumpet player. Well, I mean, is he daddy? He's daddy. Well, that's where I got my learning from.

Willie Senior plays clarinet. Yeah. He's still alive. And the young boy. Young Willie, he's with Paul Barberin. Jim Humphrey was the name of the old grandfather. The trumpet player. Oh, what, his daddy? Yeah. We call him Mr. Willie.
No, listen, there's Willie Junior, he plays clarinet. Willie Senior plays clarinet, and the grandfather named Jim Humphrey, and the grandfather named
Jim Humphrey, and the grandfather named Jim Humphrey, and the grandfather named Jim Humphrey played trumpet. I know that.
I know that. Yeah, I know that.

I know that. I know that. Or he played trombone. Yeah, but there's a mess. There's so many of them. They're all great too. Well, what was this big boy, a great big fella, he's a humphrey too. Is he kind of a relation to that? Well, I was just a guy.
I was just a guy. I was just a guy. to them? Which one? Percy. Percy? The trumpet? Yeah, yeah. Yeah, that's his, that's really union. I met him sometime, but I didn't know him. He was young, I guess.

It was his father or his grandfather, you think, that you studied? Oh. See, both of them played and taught music too. They're all music teachers. Well, he's teaching now, this poor. I saw him in Miami, see, he was teaching. Yeah, well, this ball's been teaching, I guess, sometime. Can you remember your very first job here in the city?
Well, yes. It was out at, out on, way out at St. Thomas and... I forget that other street now. I know it was in a lawn, a big lawn, yeah, Jackie.

Was that me and the channel? Oh, the channel, yeah. But it was on St. Thomas Street and some other street. That's where my first job was, in New Orleans. From that play, that Saturday night I think it was, and that Sunday night we went to St. Elizabeth Hall. And then we was off for a week I think, then we went to Biloxi, Gulfport, and on like that. We got a job at National Park, you know, just kept going.

What was that first job? Was that a lawn party? A lawn party, that's what I mean, yeah, a lawn party. Somebody told me once something that you played your first job at a ball game or something, you don't remember. What? Baseball game or something. You don't remember anything about that. I remember playing, but that wasn't my first job.

That wasn't your first job. Oh yeah, I remember playing at a baseball game, but that wasn't my first job. Yeah, I believe there was other colored park out there, National Park. Used to play ball there too, see, big dances.
That's the National Park, yeah. Got a big school out there now. What about brass bands and parades? Did you play many parades? Oh Lord, yeah.

Lots of them. I had a club called The Buzzards. Yeah. I played for them every column. Every column. When I finished this column, you make a contract for the next column. That's true. And one thing I must say, I left kind of on a sudden there, see, and I had to contract for them and I could never come back. But I don't see none of them. That Gundolfa fella, I'll tell you about that, he was the head of that. Well that's still going.
John Casimir has been marching for them every column.

But I mean the fella I always played, I didn't find out that John, John, Gundolfa, anyway, Gundolfa. Joe Gundolfa, I asked you about it. They have different bands every Saturday night. Yeah, I should play out on the lake for them all, every Sunday, pretty much when you didn't have to play a parade or something, but down the street show. But see how it goes them days, if you signed a contract with a man there for advertising and another man wants you for a parade, why don't you just call up some of the other musicians and get them to play this and play that? That's all they used to do, see. Buddy Petit could get you with that. He'd get three jobs in one night. The fella going around looking for Buddy with a gun in his pocket. He seemed not to see him, he would kill him, you know. And they walk up on Buddy, Buddy used to food some kind of stuff called luck, you know. And go to spittin', see what he needs you. He said, Buddy, I said, pshw, look at that. I told that fella, I forgot I had that job and I put another fella over there, but I beat on there afterwards. He said, well alright, you come on around there, Buddy, go up there and blow a couple of tunes and leaves and go to another job. Boy, he was a kid up Buddy Petit. What was luck? I don't know except I know what he did. They had a place called the Royal Garden Hall, right there Grab and Ramp Hall. That was his name Royal Garden, on this side of the street. And we wasn't working there. One fella playing up there from over the river, I don't know who he was, so Buddy said, I'm going to get that job. I said, how you going to get it? I'll get it, I'll show you something when I get that job. I went up there, we went to spitting and talking to the man, the man said, hey, you come next Sunday Saturday. That's true. Some kind of stuff, he's putting his mouth and spit his mouth. I said, I don't understand, luck he taught him. He gave him good luck? He must have given him good luck. He waited all the time, time he was ready for a job, he went and got it. Oh, that's true.
You better get some of it. I didn't ever know what it was. I didn't never know what it was. Too bad we never will know. Maybe something, is it that in your book, Barbara, that you read? Luck powder?
Yeah, or something that you chew. It doesn't say anything about chewing it, but they sure sell it over at the Cracker Jacks. Yeah, up there on that pole.
How many guys?

Well, I was on a show last year and a fella had the show. They used to shoot dice. And that man used to lift something in his hand all the time. And he went all the money all the time. Tell you his hand switched. I have to put this pot in my hand, my hand switched, you know. And they put that pot in and boy. He had loaded dice, that would put the food down. Well, it might have been loaded dice too. But I'm telling you, he won all the money every time he shoots dice, he won all the money.
Well, did, did Barthede cook this powder on his hands too? Yeah, he put it all the money. He chewed it and he put it on his hands both.
Yeah, but he had something to put it in his mouth too. Wow. Something like gum. Yeah. But it was black.
Did he tell you where he got it?

He never did tell me. He just tell me I'm going to get a job and say, if you don't believe, come with me now. Sure you're not. But I knew he was using something. I knew he was using something. He didn't walk up and get a job that easy. Yeah. Right. These brass bands, were they your bands?
Did you organize them or did you play in other people's bands too? Well, I had one myself. You had one? I had one for that Connler. I had one for that Connler.
I didn't have one like, I mean like the old Tuxedo and them bands. They were standard bands. But I had one every year when we get there for a parade, I had one ready. See, I know.
Get some extra names. Did you play in some of those other bands like the Onward or Tuxedo or? Well, I played a few of them.
I mean, parades like that for Elks and things like that.
When was the last year you played in a parade? When was the last year you played in a parade?

Oh, one of the last times I played in a parade was, the last parade I played was in Chicago. Elks Convention. That was the last one I played, but the last one I played was in 1925. But they had a big Elks Convention in Chicago in 47 or 48, something like that. And we got up with brass band there and played parade. They had about 40 or 50 bands. They had bands, parades, took like seven miles. Did any of them swing? And see what was guiding with us, we won't play no marches. We were just swinging. Boy, we was cleaning up. We won't play no marches. We couldn't play no marches. We didn't know nothing. And we was just cutting the blues, St. Louis Blues, and all the hard society and all that that. Had a lot of fellas from New Orleans that were playing and playing. Made a nice parade there. I had Lee Collin in the band with me on trumpet. And I forget now, I got any of them from New Orleans. I can't think of where all they was, man.
Anybody like Cubby Hall on drums? Did you ever play with them? Cubby? Yeah, I do. Or his brother? I was wondering about somebody at that.
Did you know Jimmy Blank, the piano player?

Sure. Sure, I know him. Where was he from? Do you remember anybody? Tell him he's from Milwaukee. I don't know. I don't know. Guys, that guy didn't tell you where the real home was. But we had a fella named Ed Ellis used to play trombone. Talked properly, you know. Every time somebody asked him, he was a little bit of a guitar.

I was wondering about somebody at that. Did you know Jimmy Blank, the piano player? Sure. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. But stuff says New York. So I asked him again, he says, tell him my home is in Philly. So he got sick, see. And he got really sick. Didn't nobody know what to do for everybody. So where was his people and everything. So he called his wife. His wife was named Stella. He said, what is it? He said, I told you all my home was in Philly and I told you all my home was in New York. He said, but I wish you'd call my mother down in Atlanta, Georgia and tell him I'm about to die. Daddy? Yeah, he called me. Daddy's home is in Atlanta, see. I always said, I'm from Philly and New York. Daddy stuff See I'm older than him you know. He's older than him. One time in Chicago he was playing at the Garrett Ball you know. And so I was playing on the side. So we all had an intermission. So he come and said Punch, I want you to tell these guys, they think I'm old. I said look old. Tell them about how old you think I am. I told him I said he was about 33. And Boyd says oh man you know Willie Allen older than that. I said no he's a young fella. Where do you want to get them wrinkles out of his face then? Well he's a young fella. Guy Kelly and Ray Allen come along together see. And Lee Collin. Them three come behind. Buddy 15 and me and Louie and Chris Kelly and Sam Morgan all of them in front of them. That's true. Just like Buddy Bowling was in front of me. I didn't know them both. I didn't know King Oliver until I went to Chicago and so on. I didn't know them.
I believe he left there in 22 didn't he? Joe, I think before then, 1918. Yeah, I didn't know him. He was in the Army when he left here again. Sure, I didn't know him.
What's the earliest thing you remember? I was wondering. Do you remember the Spanish American War or any of those things?
No, I don't know World War I. I don't know the Spanish War. Do you remember? I mean anything, any big event you know?
War? Well, any songs you remember that came out of your earliest memories? I was wondering what, you know, some of the different songs and music you heard and that bunch of.

Well, I'll tell you, before I went to the Army I didn't hear nothing but blues and things like that. When I went to the Army I liked them Army songs, like Over There, you know, Alexander's Ragtime Bay and all them kind of songs. But before I went to the Army I didn't remember a lot of blues and things, see? Because that's all that's clean here. Just one blues to another blues. Well, after a while, you just know the guys playing high society, and Planet Marvill, That's A Plenty, Banana Peeling, and all them kind of numbers, you know, Tag, Tag, Rag, and Panama Rag, all them different kind of songs like that, you know?
Banana Peeling? Yeah. What's that? It was a stump number.
Never heard of a stump number. Do you remember how it feels a little bit? No. I know the last part of it. That's the last part of it. Yeah. How much one would I have to dig up?

Well, it was, it was, it was one of the, you know, one of the numbers. Do you remember about the first record that you ever made? I believe the first record I was made was Black But Sweet Old Gold. With the Macs. Macs. Was that made up in Chicago or down here? Right here. Right here.
Right here. Remember the studio, where it was cut?

I forgot where that was, but I don't believe it was on Cornell Street. I believe it was on either Barone or Carnell Street, something like that. It probably was Barone. Hmm? Probably was Barone, because I think Manuel Moneta made some records at the same time.
Yeah, that's what I think it was. Who would you piano play on there? There's a piano and trumpet. Piano and trumpet.
I mean, you're the trumpet.
You're the trumpet, but I'm trying to remember what else is there.
Oh, there was some old piano by the name of Henry Brown. Oh, he was the one at the show. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He was another great blues man.

There's a Henry Brown that plays blues living in St. Louis now. Can you see him? I don't know. I don't know. I'll tell you how I find out about it. Roosevelt Sykes told me about it, you know. Might be him.
I don't know. Never got to know his father from Atlanta. Well, he died pretty soon. His name was Hemingway, James Hemingway. He played with us a couple of years, but he didn't live alone. He died.
Was he a trumpet player? No, piano. Piano player.
Nice piano player. When you played with Jelly Roll did you ever make any records with him? No, I didn't.

He didn't make no while I was with him. He had made some before I got with him. But I don't think he made no more after that. Because he died right after I got out of the band, me and Swayze. He didn't live long. But I heard all his records, Dr. Jazz and all that kind of stuff. But I didn't make any with him. He never made any records? The only guy that made records was Tiny Pong, Al Wynn, Jimmy Wade. He was a big chief. And what this guy named in New York, uh, the trombones. He's an Indian. Big chief. Oh, you made some boy? That's right, in New York. Yeah, that's right. In New York, you made. That's the last records I made in 48. I remember. The time he had all that snow in there.
Yeah, Bunk was there that year too. The Bunk sure was.
I was down the house for a couple of days, about 48 inches of snow or something. Oh, it was.
Two days' time. Boy, they had some snow there. You couldn't see nobody on the side of the street. Yeah. It was stacked up.
Did you make some records with Big Bill Bruinsy, the blues singer? Did you ever play on Big Bill? Big Bill, the blues singer.

Oh, yeah. I made a record with him by the, she's the trucking mother for you. Oh, yeah. Yeah, I made a record with him. I sure did, I swear to God. She's the trucking mother for you. Well, you couldn't forget that. No, no.
Well, so I made that in Chicago. Yeah. I thought you were on some of those. Did you make very many with him or just a couple?
I made a couple with him and I made some with this guy to put a harmonica in the guitar. What do you mean? Y'all want him too. Not even one? No, but it would be New York, Sonny Terry Williams.
Hmm? Joe Williams. No, no. Sonny Terry in New York. You never made a place.
No, I don't know his name, but I can't call it now. Sonny Boy Williams? Mm-mm. Wait. Let's see. Who's some harmonica players?
Roosevelt.
He named Roosevelt, I think. Roosevelt? He named Roosevelt, I think. Roosevelt?

Or Martin? Yeah, he named him. I think it was a couple of good harmonica. Down on the south side of Chicago, remember? That's too late, you know. Of course there was little Walter, but those fellows came up after you left. Yeah, this guy's named Roosevelt. I can't think his first name. We'll try to find out who it is someday.
We'll look it up. We'll look it up. We'll look it up. We'll look it up. He plays harmonic on his neck and he plays guitar.
I see no stuff
I've seen those things, but I never heard about his records.

Oh yeah, man. He's still making records. But I can't think of his first name now. Jazz Piuma? I'll play some one. He lived right at 35th and State. Tampa Red used to live along in there. That's the man I'm trying to call, Tampa Ray. But, but, but, but, uh, never to call him Tampa Ray. Yeah. But his real name is Roosevelt. Oh, is that right? I never do. Yeah. Tampa Ray, yes then. I thought his name was Hudson Whittaker. He put a harmonic in his mouth and put a guitar back there. I thought his name was Hudson Whittaker. No, Tampa Ray. That's, that's, that's the right.

No, then Mama Yancey used to call him Mrs. She'd meet and say, I saw Mrs. Tampa over at the market yesterday at the store. Mrs. Tampa. He used to record for Lester Melrose, and Lester always owed him royalties and so on. They'd get together. Yeah.

Do you remember the tunes you cut with Tampa Red? Well, I can't call the name of them. Some blues I know. Well, we'll look them up someday. Yeah, let's look them up. You see my name on there, all right?
Yeah, well, Bill, you don't have orange book on them? Oh, it's in the back room. We'll get it. We'll get it. Yeah, we'll get it. Yeah. Did you ever work on any river boats, anything?
Well, I left here one time on Saturday, coming back Tuesday. You told me.
Yeah, you said it on the other day. But any other, any other things besides that, your job or things? No. I just wondered, since they put you in that.

Taylor, one thing I can say, we did Oz with a show by the name of Charlie Taylor. We got in some town up in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and we was off, and some man hired the band, you know, and we played on the boat all night's after night.
